paper_title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

We propose ExRL, sample-efficient RL method for adapting long-chunk policies through execution-length control. Left: Existing RL methods lose sample efficiency as action chunks grow longer, while ExRL maintains high learning efficiency. Right: ExRL improves π0.5 policies to high success rates on contact-rich and long-horizon real-world tasks with only tens of minutes of physical interaction or few hundred episodes. AbstractPredicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space lowdimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), simple approach which augments the base policy with lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sampleefficient adaptation of diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning. I. INTRODUCTION Robot policies trained on demonstration datasets have enabled increasingly complex and generalizable behaviors across wide range of robotic control tasks [57, 1]. key technique shared by many of these policies is action chunking [70]. Rather than predicting single action at each query, actionchunked policies predict sequence of actions and execute them open-loop, which can help capture non-Markovian structure in demonstrations [32, 39] and reduce compounding errors [32, 68]. common choice in recent robot policies is to predict long action chunks, often exceeding 20 steps and approaching 50, as in vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0.5 [9] and π0-FAST [48], and world action models such as DreamZero [65]. By producing many actions per model query, long chunks enable high-frequency control (e.g., 50 Hz) for dexterous tasks such as laundry folding [8], while reducing inference pauses for smoother, faster execution. These long-chunk robot policies, while performant, are rarely optimal when deployed in the real world due to limited demonstration coverage and imperfect generalization [55]. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides direct way to adapt these policies from online experience. In other domains such as language modeling, online RL has been shown to be quite effective for adapting models pretrained on offline datasets [45, 24, 21]. For robotic control, however, online data collection in the real world is often slow, costly, and sometimes unsafe, making sample efficiency central requirement. Yet we observe that long action chunks introduce major bottleneck for sample-efficient adaptation (Figure 1, left). RL methods that optimize entire action chunks or their latent variables face an increasingly high-dimensional optimization space as the chunk length grows. This substantially increases the amount of online experience required for adaptation. This motivates us to seek an adaptation interface whose dimensionality does not grow with the chunk length. We observe that action-chunked policies naturally expose such an interface, namely, how long to execute predicted chunk before querying the policy again. Although execution length is simple scalar decision, adapting it to the current state and predicted action chunk can substantially alter policy behavior by controlling the trade-off between longer openloop execution, which better exploits the benefits of action chunking, and shorter execution, which improves responsiveness to unexpected state changes or dynamics mismatch [39]. This makes execution length meaningful variable for policy improvement, while being particularly attractive for long chunks: as the chunk size grows, the number of possible execution lengthsand hence the expressivityincreases, whereas the optimization itself remains low-dimensional discrete problem. We instantiate this idea as Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), sample-efficient online RL method for adapting long-chunk policies. It adds lightweight execution-length policy that selects how many actions from each predicted chunk to execute before replanning, and trains it using standard off-policy RL algorithms. Because this adapter can be learned without modifying the base policy itself, ExRL provides policy-agnostic interface that can be applied to virtually any class of action-chunked policies. Execution-length control is ultimately bounded by the capabilities of the underlying base policy. To go beyond this limitation, we can further optionally distill successful online trajectories back into the base policy during RL using simple imitation loss, allowing the base policy itself to improve alongside the adapter. Finally, ExRL can also leverage general offline data, such as human demonstrations, by reinterpreting arbitrary trajectory segments as off-policy experience under different execution lengths, further improving online sample efficiency. largely without We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ExRL across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, showing state-of-the-art online adaptation performance across range of long-chunk policies, task-specific hyperparameter tuning. These include standard action-chunked policies, different classes of pretrained VLA models such as π0.5 [9] and π0-FAST [48], as well as world action model, Cosmos Policy [28]. On real-world tasks spanning precise manipulation, long-horizon coordination, and clothing folding, ExRL efficiently adapts frozen π0.5 policies, approaching perfect success on cube stacking with about ten minutes of physical interaction. II. RELATED WORK Imitation learning in robotics. Imitation learning, particularly behavior cloning, has been widely used to train datadriven policies for robotic control [5, 51, 69, 18, 52]. Prior work has explored wide range of action parameterizations and policy architectures for imitation learning. Earlier methods often represent actions with Gaussian or GMM policies [25, 41], while more recent approaches use expressive generative modeling techniques, including VAEs [70], diffusion or flow models [14, 44, 8, 7], and autoregressive next-token prediction models [72, 27, 48]. With the growing scale of human demonstration datasets and policy models [60, 26, 11, 46], imitation learning has further become pretraining paradigm for generalist robot policies, absorbing broad prior knowledge into single model that can be adapted for real-world deployment [44, 27, 8]. Our work provides an efficient method to adapt these diverse policy classes from online experience. Adaptive execution of action chunks. Action chunking, as used in ACT [70], has become de facto design choice in robot policies learned with imitation learning. Recognizing that the execution length of action chunks strongly affects policy behavior [54, 68, 39], several concurrent works have explored adaptive execution strategies. Earlier RL methods such as Dynamic Action Repetition [31] and TempoRL [6] adapt how long primitive action is repeated, rather than how much of predicted action chunk is executed. AAC [36] selects the execution length of vision-language-action models using action entropy, while FFDC [61] selects the execution length for world action models using learned verifier to check whether predicted future observations remain consistent with the real rollout. ExRL instead learns execution-length decisions directly from task rewards through online RL. TAS [63] uses online RL to select among actions cached from overlapping chunks at every timestep, rather than explicitly learning chunk-level execution length. Two other recent works, ACSAC [13] and ACH [53], learn value-based adaptive chunk-size selection for offline-to-online RL. However, these methods train and evaluate specific chunked policies within offline and offline-to-online RL frameworks, and are not designed as plug-in adapters for arbitrary pretrained actionchunked policies. The closest work to ours is [71], concurrent study that also adapts action-chunked policies through reinforcement learning over execution length. However, it relies on PPO for optimization; our comparison in Appendix shows that off-policy learning can adapt execution lengths with substantially fewer online samples. Reinforcement learning for robot policy adaptation. Onpolicy methods such as PPO and GRPO have been used to finetune pretrained robot policies [34, 40, 12, 50], but often require many online rollouts, limiting their practicality on real robots. Off-policy RL algorithms such as SAC [22] and TD3 [20] can use data more efficiently, but their standard implementations typically use deterministic or Gaussian actors, making direct adaptation of more complex generative policies nontrivial. Policy-specific approaches address this challenge in different ways: DSRL [59] and ZPRL [66] optimize diffusion/flow policies in latent spaces. OGPO [47] uses off-policy critics to guide optimization of the diffusion or flow generation process, while RL-100 [33] applies PPO-style updates across diffusion denoising steps. These methods can improve sample efficiency, but remain tied to particular policy classes. Residual RL instead learns additive corrections to the base actions [67, 4, 3, 16, 56]. While policy-agnostic and lightweight, residual RL still requires continuous action optimization; correcting an entire chunk makes this space grow with chunk length. RL Token [64] learns lightweight actor conditioned on VLA representations and reference chunks, with regularization toward the base actions. PA-RL [42] achieves policy-agnostic adaptation by casting RL as action optimization followed by supervised policy learning. RECAP [2] builds an offline-toonline pipeline for training advantage-conditioned policies, which can incorporate batch online RL [17] for efficient adaptation. In contrast to these action-modifying approaches, ExRL adapts the execution length of each predicted chunk, reducing online adaptation to compact discrete decision space and enabling sample-efficient, policy-agnostic adaptation. ExRL can improve policies without changing the actions proposed within each chunk, but its capability is ultimately bounded by the underlying base policy. How can we go beyond this limitation? We note that, by replanning at adaptive times, ExRL can stitch together prefixes from different predicted chunks and produce successful trajectories that would not arise from simply executing the original long chunks open-loop. We can therefore distill these improved behaviors back into the base policy during RL (Figure 2). Specifically, from each successful ExRL rollout, we construct H-step action-chunk targets from the primitive actions actually executed, even when target spans multiple replanning decisions, and update πbase using the same behavior cloning objective as in pretraining. Leveraging offline data. ExRL can also reuse general offline trajectories, such as human demonstrations, even if they were collected without action chunking. The key observation is that any sequence of recorded primitive actions can be retrospectively treated as virtual action chunk (Figure 3). Its prefixes of different lengths then provide real experience of executing the same action sequence for different lengths. Concretely, before online training, we enumerate trajectory segments of all lengths from offline trajectories and add the corresponding execution-length transitions to the replay the offline trajectory provides buffer. For each transition, the accumulated rewards and resulting state for the executed prefix; from that state onward, the value target bootstraps with the current base policy and execution-length strategy. This anchors the value of each virtual chunk to the expected return under ExRLs actual execution strategy, rather than to the behavior that generated the offline trajectory. When online behavior cloning is enabled, demonstration data can also be mixed with successful online trajectories to jointly update the base policy. Remark. One may ask why we do not simply use short fixed execution length for previous RL methods to avoid high-dimensional optimization, or first select the optimal fixed execution length and then optimize on top of it. Always using short execution length for RL, however, can be problematic for several reasons: it may yield very poor initial performance on some tasks, making RL optimization difficult; it requires more frequent policy queries, increasing training cost and inference overhead while potentially introducing inference execution synchronization issues; and, on long-horizon tasks, it substantially increases the effective decision horizon, further complicating RL. Alternatively, preselecting an optimal fixed execution length instead requires extensive real-world evaluation, potentially hundreds of rollouts, which is already comparable to the interaction budget of typical real-world online RL experiment. V. EXPERIMENTS The goal of our experiments is to answer the following core questions: (Q1) Can ExRL enable sample-efficient adaptation across action-chunked policies, including generalist robot policies in both simulation and real-world tasks? Fig. 4. ExRL enables sample-efficient online adaptation of DP and ACT of chunk size 50 on Robomimic. Fig. 5. Online adaptation of DP on Adroit with chunk size = 32. (Q2) Can updating the base policy with successful online trajectories and demonstrations further improve adaptation? (Q3) What execution-length patterns does ExRL learn? A. Base Policies To show the generality of our method, we conduct experiments on diverse classes of action-chunked policies. We consider both representative action-chunked policies trained with imitation learning and several pretrained generalist robot policies of different classes. Representative action-chunked policies: (1) Diffusion Policy (DP) [14]: an action-chunked policy that models multimodal continuous action chunks using denoising diffusion [23]; and (2) ACT [70]: transformer-based policy that predicts action chunks using an encoderdecoder architecture. Generalist robot policies. (1) π0 [8] and π0.5 [9]: state-of-theart VLA models that use flow matching [37] to model action chunks; (2) π0-FAST [48]: an autoregressive VLA model that generates action chunks through efficient action tokenization; and (3) Cosmos Policy [28]: world action model built on large pretrained video generation model. B. Baselines and Setup We compare ExRL against execution-length baselines and several online adaptation baselines, with focus on policyagnostic methods for action-chunked policies. Our baselines include: Execution-length baselines. (1) Random-k: randomly samples an execution length from the feasible set at each policy query; (2) Optimal fixed-k: sweeps fixed execution lengths and reports the best-performing one. AAC [36]: training-free adaptive execution method that selects the execution length using action entropy. Online BC: An ablation that directly distills successful online rollouts back into the base policy using behavior cloning without RL. Policy Decorator [67]: An off-policy residual RL method that freezes the base policy and learns additive corrections to its predicted actions, with bounded residuals and controlled exploration for stable online learning. DSRL [59]: latent steering method for diffusionand flowbased policies that keeps the base policy frozen and applies RL in its initial latent-noise space rather than directly modifying the generated actions. PA-RL [42]: policy-agnostic RL finetuning method that uses learned critic to improve action candidates through reranking and local optimization, and then distills the improved actions back into the base policy. OGPO [47]: An off-policy full-finetuning method for diffusionand flow-based policies. It learns off-policy critics for data reuse and uses their values to optimize the full diffusion or flow generation process through modified PPO objective. ResFiT [3]: demo-augmented residual RL method that keeps the base policy frozen, constrains residual magnitude for stable exploration, and jointly trains on demonstration and online data; we adapt its original per-step residual formulation to operate over action chunks. DICE-RL [56]: Also demo-augmented residual RL method that combines value-guided action selection with selective behavior regularization to reinforce high-value behaviors while remaining close to the pretrained policy. On Robomimic, the main experiments use = 50 for DP and ACT; Appendix Figure 13 reports additional = 32 results for both policies. Following prior work [59, 47], we use base-policy checkpoints that leave meaningful headroom for RL improvement. Our goal on these benchmarks is not to maximize base-policy performance, but to use them as controlled testbed for evaluating long-chunk policy adaptation. For each variant of ExRL, we keep most hyperparameters fixed across tasks and make only few task-level adjustments when necessary, such as the discount factor γ and network width. Appendix provides task details, policy architectures, baseline adaptations, and hyperparameter settings. For each run in the plot, we report the average success rate and 95% confidence intervals over three seeds. C. Sample-Efficient Adaptation in Simulation Figures 4, 5, and 6 show that ExRL substantially improves frozen base policies, often reaching success rates close to 100% by learning only the execution length. The gains over the optimal fixed-k baseline are particularly large on DP Can, Square, and Tool Hang, and across all four LIBERO policies. As these improvements require no changes to the actions predicted by the base policy, they validate the importance and expressiveness of execution-length control as an adaptation interface. Compared with other RL methods, ExRL often learns substantially faster, particularly early in online adaptation. On LIBERO, for example, it improves π0.5 from nearly 0% to over 90% success within 200,000 environment steps. The advantage is also pronounced on the challenging Tool Hang task, where ExRL-SAC achieves high success with both DP and ACT; with DP, it exceeds 90% success while all other baselines remain at around 20% or below. In these settings, ExRL-Q + Online BC substantially outperforms both frozen-base ExRL-Q and Online BC alone, supporting the value of distilling the improved behaviors discovered by ExRL back into the base policy. With demonstration augmentation, ExRL-Q + Online BC rapidly reaches near-perfect success on ACT Can and all four Adroit tasks, competitive with the strongest demonstrationbased baselines. Figure 7 further isolates the benefit of demonstrations for executionlength learning: adding human experience to RL replay accelerates early adaptation on Can while keeping the base policy frozen. Fig. 7. Human demonstrations accelerate ExRL-Q on Can (H = 50). The LIBERO results also highlight the generality of ExRL. The same execution-length formulation enables efficient adaptation of flow-based VLAs, autoregressive VLAs, and world action model, despite their substantially different architectures and action-generation processes. D. Sample-Efficient Real-World Adaptation We further adapt π0.5 with chunk size = 50 on four real-world tasks (Figure 1, right; Table I). Power insertion requires contact-rich manipulation, while clothing folding involves manipulating deformable objects. Both clothing folding and parts organization require long-horizon coordination. We Fig. 9. How ExRL adapts execution length. (a) Mean execution lengths during free motion and near interaction, with 95% trajectory-bootstrap intervals. (b) Planned vertical motion over rejected and accepted full chunks on Square; gray shows the median and 1090% range of rejected proposals. (c) In another Square rollout, short executions progressively align the nut with the peg before ExRL selects long execution. report success rate for stacking, folding, and insertion, and the fraction of completed stages for organization. Further setup details are provided in Appendix A-G. The sample efficiency of ExRL carries over to real-world adaptation. With the base policy frozen, ExRL-Q approaches 100% success on stack cube with only ten minutes of physical interaction, and reaches nearly 90% on the long-horizon clothing folding task within 85 minutes. Power insertion and parts organization similarly improve within few hundred rollouts. Final evaluations show substantial gains over fixedlength execution across all four tasks (Table I). E. Ablation Studies Accounting for the selected execution length in reward accumulation and discounting improves learning over TD target that treats each decision as single step (Figure 8, leftmost panel). The predicted chunk is also essential to the decision: conditioning on both the observation and the chunk raises success from around 30% to nearly 90% compared with observations alone (second panel). Thus, the critic benefits from knowing what the base policy proposes, beyond the current state. Allowing = 0 offers little additional benefit over positive execution lengths (third panel), while similar learning curves across network widths from 128 to 2048 suggest that ExRL does not require precise tuning of network capacity (rightmost panel). F. What Execution Length Patterns Does ExRL Learn? ExRL improves policy without changing its predicted actions, raising the question of how execution-length decisions reshape its behavior. Figure 9(a) reveals consistent pattern: across Lift, Can, Square, and real-world insertion, ExRL selects shorter executions near the object or target than during free motion. The mean length roughly halves in simulation and falls to about quarter on real-world insertion. ExRL therefore concentrates replanning near interaction, while allowing longer motions elsewhere. Short executions, however, need not serve the same purpose. Two Square rollouts illustrate how ExRL decides when to continue with longer chunk. In Figure 9(b), it repeatedly truncates unsuitable predictions with little physical motion, then accepts chunk that predicts useful grasp-and-lift motion. Here, frequent replanning provides new candidate motions from nearly the same state. In Figure 9(c), short executions instead change the state through small corrections, bringing the nut closer to the peg before ExRL switches to longer execution. The distinction is between waiting for useful prediction and moving into state from which longer prediction becomes useful. Both behaviors depend on the current state and the proposed chunk, rather than fixed preference for short execution. Figure 17 in the appendix illustrates how this balance unfolds across four real-world tasks. Further analysis shows that shuffling the same execution lengths across states and chunks reduces success (Appendix D-B). It also suggests complementary reason to preserve longer execution: under feature aliasing, locally similar policy features can repeatedly produce similar first actions, so frequent replanning may interrupt useful progression through chunk (Appendix D-C). VI. CONCLUSION We introduced ExRL, which shifts online adaptation of long-chunk policies from action generation to execution-length control. Conditioning this scalar decision on the state and predicted chunk provides substantial behavioral flexibility, while keeping optimization low-dimensional as chunk size grows. Across simulation and real-world tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient improvement of diverse frozen policies, often surpassing their best fixed execution length. Online imitation learning and offline demonstrations further extend these gains and support continued base-policy improvement during RL. These findings show that learning how to execute policys predictions can unlock capabilities already present in the policy, making execution length practical interface for adapting long-chunk robot policies with limited online interaction. VII. LIMITATIONS Our real-world experiments keep the base policy frozen and do not yet incorporate online BC. Performance therefore remains constrained by the actions the base policy can propose, and several tasks still fall short of 100% success. Extending online BC to these experiments may help address the remaining failures. We also adapt each task separately and have not evaluated joint multi-task adaptation or generalization to unseen tasks. Recent work demonstrates that sufficiently diverse multi-task experience and value-based RL can improve performance on unseen scenes and objects in simulation [29]; whether execution-length adaptation offers similar benefits remains open. Finally, we have not tested ExRL together with asynchronous inference methods such as real-time chunking (RTC) [10]. Understanding how adaptive replanning interacts with overlapping inference and execution is an important direction for extending ExRL to latency-sensitive deployments.
